messages:
mike: Heads-up — ran a perf sweep on the continuous batching path with tool/function calls enabled. Seeing a 18-25% drop in tokens/sec for long-lived sessions when a tool pause occurs mid-decode. attaching quick profiler notes. :eyes:
anya: ugh. is that the pause causing KV cache churn or just batch formation waiting?
kevin: my first guess is queue hang + token-budget miss. When a tool call inserts a blocking op, we hold the whole decode batch waiting for the tool result, which pushes other requests past their token budget and forces smaller kernel choices.
sara: does the profiler show more kernel switches around the pause boundary? that would explain extra overhead.
mike: yes — stack shows repeated kernel selection and small-launch overhead after resume. profiler snippet: `kernel_select: 74->128 tokens, 3 switches in 120ms window`
anya: hmm. so post-pause we often fall back from vectorized matmul to slower path because sequence length distribution changed?
kevin: exactly. also noticed KV cache miss rates spike — likely because some batches are resumed on different workers which don't have the cached KV.
mike: experiment log: run A (no tool calls) = 12.4k tokens/s; run B (tool pauses enabled) = 9.8k tokens/s; run C (tool pauses but enforced token-budget cap + early-flush) = 11.6k tokens/s.
sara: what was the early-flush rule?
mike: if a batch contains any active tool pause, and waiting time > 40ms OR current max tokens + queued_tokens >= token_budget_target, flush the unaffected subset early. config snippet we used:
```
queue_policy: {
  max_wait_ms: 40,
  token_budget_target: 1024,
  allow_early_flush_on_tool_pause: true,
  prefer_cohosted_kv: true
}
```
kevin: important: prefer_cohosted_kv attempts to keep resumed requests on the same worker that owns the KV to avoid cache misses. It requires the router to be KV-aware.
anya: did early-flush cause any regression in latency p95 for short requests?
mike: small bump (~4ms) for 95th on short gen (<64 tokens), but overall throughput and p50 improved. tradeoff seems acceptable for our SLA.
sara: what about stop-token handling? tool calling sometimes hits stop tokens (tool should intercept). Are we delaying decode because we wait for stop-token confirmation across batch?
mike: yes — current decode loop treats stop tokens as per-batch boundary. When one request hits stop and triggers a tool, the entire batch waits for tool pause resolution to apply structured output injection. That’s a big source of stalls.
kevin: potential fix: make stop-token handling request-local inside batch. i.e., let other requests continue generating while paused request is detached and moved to a holding micro-batch. Might complicate KV and kernel assumptions but could cut stalls.
anya: that would need ability to splice KV streams mid-batch. Does runtime support pausing a single stream without flushing whole batch cache?
kevin: not today. we'd need to snapshot per-request KV pointers and let the remaining streams continue with shared cache. Complexity: kernel code assumes contiguous sequences across lanes.
sara: maybe a simpler heuristic: if a batch has >1 active lane and 1 triggers tool pause, and queued tokens for remaining lanes >= min_batch_tok, then early-flush remaining lanes immediately. That avoids splitting kernels but reduces stalls.
mike: that's what run C did — it only detaches when remaining queued_tokens >= 128.
anya: we should also add instrumentation: log when a batch flush is driven by tool pause, and whether the resumed request hit a KV cache-miss. then we can correlate miss->worker-affinity.
kevin: +1. also add metric: kernel_switch_count per-request, and per-batch token_budget_utilization.
sara: another idea: for tool-heavy workloads, use a conservative token_budget_target (lower) and shorter max_wait_ms to keep batches small and reduce the probability one lane blocks many others. cost vs throughput tradeoff though.
mike: noted. I also saw a regression related to the scheduler's worker fallback: when kernel selection fails on preferred fast kernel (quantized path) we fall back to generic kernel but keep the same batch size, which increases per-token latency. maybe downgrade batch size when fallback occurs.
kevin: we can implement a dynamic batch_size_adjustment: if fallback_count > threshold in last N batches, reduce batch max_tokens by 25% for next window.
anya: will that destabilize p95? need canary.
sara: let's sketch an A/B: current, early-flush heuristic (run C), and batch_size_adj on fallback. measure tokens/s, p50, p95, KV_miss_rate, kernel_switch_count. keep them running for 2 hours.
mike: I'll wire the instrumentation and upload the metric dashboard. Also adding two experiment flags: `runtime.early_flush_tool_pause` and `runtime.dynamic_batch_adjust_on_fallback`.
deploy-bot: deploy queued: feature flags pushed to staging at 1769705590.
infra-bot: note: prefer_cohosted_kv requires small router change, pinging @kevin for rollout plan.
kevin: I’ll draft the router change. plan: add soft affinity header so router prefers workers with KV for that session; fall back after 3 attempts. avoids hard binds.
anya: sweet. one more: update evals to include structured outputs that cause frequent short tool calls so we don't regress on this path.
mike: agreed. action items: mike -> add metrics + dashboard; kevin -> router affinity PR; sara -> define evals for tool-heavy scenarios; anya -> run the canaries and report. I'll post results here in ~4 hours. :thumbsup:
